question.title: Billing Account Assignment
question.scenario: You created a new project for a development team, but they cannot create any billable resources like Compute Engine VMs.
question.question-text: What is the most likely cause of this issue?

choices.choice: No billing account is linked to the project
The Compute Engine API is not enabled
The project quota has been exceeded
The users lack the compute.instances.create permission

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A newly created project must be linked to a billing account before any paid resources can be provisioned. Without billing, creation requests for charged services are rejected.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The most likely cause is that no billing account is linked to the project (A). Google Cloud requires an active billing account association before any resource that incurs charges can be created. While the other options are plausible blockers, the scenario says the project was just created and the team cannot create any billable resources, which points directly to a missing billing link rather than a missing API (B), exceeded quota (C), or a permissions gap (D). API enablement errors produce a different message, quotas would only apply if resources already exist, and IAM issues would reference a specific permission denial.

ul.li: You link a billing account to a project with gcloud billing projects link PROJECT_ID --billing-account=BILLING_ACCOUNT_ID. The caller needs the billing.resourceAssociations.create permission on the billing account and resourcemanager.projects.createBillingAssignment on the project.

A project can have at most one billing account at a time. Changing the billing account does not affect existing resources but changes where future charges accrue. Removing billing disables all paid services after a grace period.

Free-tier eligible resources (e.g., f1-micro in select regions, small Cloud Storage amounts) may still require billing to be enabled, because the free tier is implemented as billing credits applied to a linked billing account.

The Billing Account Administrator role (roles/billing.admin) grants full control over a billing account, including linking it to projects. For least privilege, use Billing Account User (roles/billing.user) which only allows linking existing accounts to projects.

question.title: Managed Instance Groups
question.scenario: You need to deploy a web application that automatically scales based on CPU utilization and replaces unhealthy instances.
question.question-text: Which resource should you create to achieve automatic scaling and self-healing?

choices.choice: Individual VM instances with startup scripts
Managed instance group with autoscaling policy

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only one Compute Engine construct combines automatic creation of identical VMs from a template, metric-based autoscaling, and health-check-driven autohealing in a single resource.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A managed instance group (MIG) with an autoscaling policy (C) provides both automatic scaling and self-healing. The MIG creates identical VM instances from an instance template and uses autoscaling policies to add or remove instances based on CPU utilization, load balancing metrics, or custom Cloud Monitoring metrics. Autohealing uses HTTP health checks to detect and automatically recreate unhealthy instances. Individual VMs (A) have no scaling or healing automation. Unmanaged instance groups (B) are collections of heterogeneous VMs without autoscaling or autohealing. An instance template alone (D) is a blueprint but does not create or manage instances by itself.

ul.li: A MIG requires an instance template that defines the VM configuration (machine type, boot disk image, network tags, startup script). Templates are immutable; to change the configuration you create a new template and perform a rolling update on the MIG, which incrementally replaces instances with minimal downtime.

Autoscaling policies support multiple signal types: CPU utilization (target percentage), HTTP load balancing serving capacity (requests per second per instance), Pub/Sub queue depth, and custom Cloud Monitoring metrics. You set min and max instance counts to bound the scaling range and avoid runaway cost.

Autohealing attaches a health check (HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP) to the MIG. If an instance fails the health check for a configurable duration (initial delay + unhealthy threshold), the MIG automatically deletes and recreates it from the current instance template, restoring the application without manual intervention.

Regional MIGs distribute instances across multiple zones within a region, providing zone-level fault tolerance. If a zone experiences an outage, the MIG redistributes instances to surviving zones up to the configured maximum, maintaining the target capacity automatically.

question.title: Cloud SQL Instance Creation
question.scenario: Your application requires a managed PostgreSQL database with automatic backups and high availability within a region.
question.question-text: Which gcloud command creates a high availability Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud SQL uses --availability-type=REGIONAL to enable high availability with a standby replica in a different zone, and --database-version to specify the engine and major version.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: gcloud sql instances create with --availability-type=REGIONAL (A) creates a high-availability Cloud SQL instance with a standby replica in a different zone for automatic failover. Option B uses non-existent "gcloud sql create" syntax and --ha flag. Option C uses a fabricated "gcloud database" command group. Option D creates a valid instance but with ZONAL availability (single zone, no automatic failover), which does not meet the high availability requirement. The --database-version flag specifies both the engine type and major version (POSTGRES_14, MYSQL_8_0, etc.).

ul.li: REGIONAL availability deploys a primary instance and a standby instance in different zones within the same region. Replication is synchronous, meaning every write is committed to both instances before being acknowledged, ensuring zero data loss on failover. Failover typically completes within 60 seconds.

ZONAL availability runs a single instance in one zone with no standby. It costs less than REGIONAL but provides no automatic failover. If the zone experiences an outage, the instance is unavailable until the zone recovers or you manually perform a zone migration.

Automatic backups are enabled by default on new Cloud SQL instances and run daily during a configurable maintenance window. You can also create on-demand backups with gcloud sql backups create and enable point-in-time recovery (PITR) for transaction-log-level granularity.

Additional important creation flags include --tier (machine type, e.g., db-custom-4-16384 for 4 vCPUs/16 GB RAM), --storage-size, --storage-auto-increase, --root-password, and --authorized-networks or --no-assign-ip with --enable-private-ip for private connectivity via VPC peering.

question.title: Container Image Building
question.scenario: You have a Dockerfile in your current directory and need to build a container image and store it in Artifact Registry.
question.question-text: Which command builds the image using Cloud Build and pushes it to Artifact Registry?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Build's submit command uploads source code to Google's infrastructure, builds the container image remotely, and pushes it to the specified registry in a single operation.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: gcloud builds submit --tag REGISTRY_PATH (C) is the correct command. It uploads your source directory to Cloud Build, builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile in the source, and automatically pushes the resulting image to the registry specified in the --tag flag. Option A uses the deprecated "gcloud container build" syntax. Option B uses local Docker (valid but not Cloud Build, and the push command is incomplete). Option D uses a non-existent "gcloud artifacts build" command. Cloud Build runs entirely in Google's infrastructure, so no local Docker daemon is required.

ul.li: Cloud Build runs on Google-managed infrastructure, so you do not need Docker installed locally. The source directory is tarred, uploaded to a Cloud Storage staging bucket, and built on a Cloud Build worker VM. Build logs stream to Cloud Logging and are visible in the Console.

The Artifact Registry image path follows the format REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/REPOSITORY_NAME/IMAGE:TAG. You must create the repository first with gcloud artifacts repositories create REPO --repository-format=docker --location=REGION before pushing images to it.

For builds more complex than a single Dockerfile, use a cloudbuild.yaml configuration file that defines multiple steps (e.g., run tests, build image, scan for vulnerabilities, deploy). Passing --config=cloudbuild.yaml instead of --tag switches Cloud Build to multi-step mode.

Cloud Build provides a free tier of 120 build-minutes per day on e2-medium machines. For faster builds, specify --machine-type=e2-highcpu-8 or e2-highcpu-32, which consume the free tier faster but complete builds more quickly. Build minutes beyond the free tier are billed per-minute.

question.title: Creating Alerts
question.scenario: You need to be notified when the CPU utilization of your Compute Engine instances exceeds 80% for more than 5 minutes.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Monitoring feature should you configure?

choices.choice: Alerting policy with a metric condition

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Monitoring's alerting policies let you define threshold conditions on metrics and automatically send notifications through configured channels when those conditions persist for a specified duration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An alerting policy with a metric condition (B) is the correct feature. You define a condition that monitors the compute.googleapis.com/instance/cpu/utilization metric, set a threshold of 0.8 (80%), configure an alignment period and duration window of 5 minutes, and attach notification channels (email, SMS, PagerDuty, Slack, etc.) to receive alerts when the condition triggers. Log-based metrics (A) derive metrics from log entries, not from infrastructure metrics like CPU. Custom dashboards (C) visualize metrics but do not send notifications. Uptime checks (D) probe endpoint availability via HTTP/TCP, not resource utilization.

ul.li: Alerting policy conditions support three comparison types: metric threshold (value exceeds/falls below a static or dynamic threshold for a duration), metric absence (no data received for a specified period), and forecast (predicted to breach a threshold within a time window). The 5-minute CPU scenario uses a threshold condition.

Notification channels must be created and verified before they can be attached to alerting policies. Supported channel types include email, SMS, PagerDuty, Slack, webhooks, and Pub/Sub. Each policy can have multiple notification channels for redundancy across communication methods.

Uptime checks send synthetic requests from global probe locations to your endpoints at configurable intervals (1, 5, 10, or 15 minutes). They monitor availability and response latency but do not measure server-side resource utilization like CPU or memory, making them complementary to metric-based alerts rather than a substitute.

Dashboards provide real-time and historical visualization of metrics using charts, gauges, scorecards, and log panels, but they are a passive monitoring tool. Combining dashboards with alerting policies gives you both proactive notification and visual drill-down for incident response.

question.title: Snapshot Management
question.scenario: You need to create a backup of a Compute Engine persistent disk before performing a risky update to the application.
question.question-text: Which gcloud command creates a snapshot of a persistent disk?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Snapshots are a top-level Compute Engine resource. The command creates the snapshot by name and references the source disk and its zone as input parameters.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: gcloud compute snapshots create my-backup --source-disk=my-disk --source-disk-zone=us-central1-a (D) is the correct syntax. Snapshots are managed under the "gcloud compute snapshots" resource group. You specify the snapshot name first, then reference the source disk and its zone. Option A uses a non-existent "gcloud backup" command. Option B uses "gcloud compute disks snapshot" which is not valid syntax. Option C uses a fabricated "gcloud disk" command. Snapshots create a point-in-time copy of the disk data and are stored as regional or multi-regional resources independent of the source disk.

ul.li: Snapshots are incremental: the first snapshot copies the entire disk, but subsequent snapshots store only the blocks that changed since the previous snapshot. This makes regular snapshots storage-efficient while providing full restore capability from any individual snapshot in the chain.

For application-consistent snapshots of a running VM, either quiesce the application (flush buffers, freeze filesystem) before snapshotting, or use the --guest-flush flag which attempts to flush the guest OS file buffers. For strongest consistency, stop the VM before creating the snapshot.

Snapshot schedules automate recurring backups using resource policies. Create a schedule with gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule, specifying frequency (hourly, daily, weekly), retention period, and storage location, then attach it to disks with gcloud compute disks add-resource-policies.

Snapshots can be used to create new persistent disks in any region, enabling cross-region migration and disaster recovery. Use gcloud compute disks create --source-snapshot=my-backup --zone=TARGET_ZONE to restore a disk from a snapshot in a different zone or region than the original.

question.title: Instance Group Updates
question.scenario: You need to update the machine type of all instances in a managed instance group with minimal downtime.
question.question-text: What is the correct process to update the machine type?

choices.choice: Create a new instance template with the new machine type and perform a rolling update
Directly modify the machine type in the existing instance template
Stop all instances, change their machine type, then start them
Delete and recreate the managed instance group with new settings

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Instance templates are immutable after creation. The standard update workflow is to create a new template and then perform a rolling update that incrementally replaces instances.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The correct process is to create a new instance template with the desired machine type and then perform a rolling update on the MIG (A). Instance templates are immutable in Google Cloud, meaning you cannot modify them after creation (eliminating B). Stopping all instances and changing them individually (C) causes full downtime and bypasses the MIG's template-based management. Deleting and recreating the MIG (D) destroys all instances simultaneously, causing maximum downtime and losing the MIG's configuration history. A rolling update incrementally replaces instances, maintaining availability throughout the process.

ul.li: Initiate a rolling update with gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update MIG_NAME --version=template=NEW_TEMPLATE. Configure --max-surge (extra instances created during update) and --max-unavailable (instances allowed to be offline simultaneously) to control the update pace and availability guarantee.

For zero-downtime updates behind a load balancer, set --max-surge=1 and --max-unavailable=0. This ensures at least one new instance is healthy before any old instance is removed, maintaining the desired capacity throughout the update. The trade-off is slower updates due to sequential replacement.

Canary updates allow testing a new template on a subset of instances before full rollout. Use --version with a target-size percentage: gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update MIG --version=template=NEW_TEMPLATE,target-size=20% to update only 20% of instances initially.

Monitor update progress with gcloud compute instance-groups managed describe MIG_NAME which shows the current version distribution, update status, and any instances stuck in an unhealthy state. If the new template causes health check failures, the rolling update pauses automatically based on the configured max-unavailable threshold.

question.title: Viewing Resource Quotas
question.scenario: Your team receives an error indicating they have exceeded a quota when trying to create new Compute Engine instances.
question.question-text: How can you view the current quota usage and limits for your project?

choices.choice: Review the Cloud Monitoring metrics dashboard
Check the billing reports for usage limits
Examine the Cloud Audit Logs for quota information
View the Quotas page in the Cloud Console or use gcloud compute project-info describe

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google Cloud has a dedicated Quotas page in the Console and CLI commands specifically designed to show current quota limits and real-time usage for each service and region.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Quotas page in IAM & Admin section of the Cloud Console (D) is the primary interface for viewing all quota limits and current usage across services. For Compute Engine specifically, gcloud compute project-info describe --project=PROJECT displays quota limits and usage for the project. Cloud Monitoring (A) can display quota metrics but is not the primary tool for viewing quota details. Billing reports (B) show cost data, not quota limits. Audit Logs (C) record API calls and administrative actions but do not display quota status information.

ul.li: Quotas are enforced per-project and often per-region. For example, a project might have a quota of 24 CPUs in us-central1 and a separate quota of 24 CPUs in europe-west1. The gcloud compute regions describe REGION command shows Compute Engine quota usage for a specific region.

To request a quota increase, use the Quotas page filter to find the specific quota, click the edit icon, enter the new requested limit, and submit the request. Most increases are approved automatically within minutes, but large increases or certain quotas may require manual review by Google.

Set up proactive quota monitoring by creating Cloud Monitoring alerting policies on the serviceruntime.googleapis.com/quota/allocation/usage metric. Alert when usage approaches 80% of the limit to prevent unexpected quota exhaustion during deployments or scaling events.

Some quotas are hard limits that cannot be increased (e.g., maximum number of VPC networks per project). Others have soft limits that can be raised on request. The Quotas page shows which quotas are adjustable and their maximum requestable values.

question.title: Firewall Rules
question.scenario: You need to allow HTTP traffic from the internet to web servers tagged with "web" while denying all other ingress traffic.
question.question-text: Which firewall rule configuration achieves this?

choices.choice: Create an ingress deny rule for all traffic except port 80
Create an egress allow rule for TCP port 80 with destination 0.0.0.0/0
Create an allow rule with no source filter targeting "web" instances
Create an ingress allow rule for TCP port 80 with source 0.0.0.0/0 and target tag "web"

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: VPC firewall rules use direction (ingress/egress), action (allow/deny), source ranges, protocols/ports, and target tags to control traffic. The implicit deny-all ingress rule handles the "deny everything else" part automatically.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An ingress allow rule for TCP port 80 with source 0.0.0.0/0 and target tag "web" (D) is the correct configuration. This allows HTTP traffic from any internet IP to reach only VMs tagged "web". The VPC's implied deny-all ingress rule automatically blocks all other inbound traffic that is not explicitly allowed, so no additional deny rule is needed. Option A is overly complex and would require enumerating all ports to exclude. Option B creates an egress rule (wrong direction for incoming traffic). Option C allows traffic from any source on any port, which is too permissive.

ul.li: Every VPC network has two implied firewall rules that cannot be deleted: deny all ingress (priority 65535) and allow all egress (priority 65535). These serve as the default-deny baseline for incoming traffic and default-allow for outgoing traffic. Explicit rules with lower priority numbers (higher priority) override these implied rules.

Network tags on VM instances determine which firewall rules apply. Tags are arbitrary strings (e.g., "web", "db", "internal") set on the instance. Target tags on firewall rules filter which VMs the rule applies to, while source tags can be used to allow traffic only from VMs with specific tags within the same VPC.

Firewall rule priority ranges from 0 (highest) to 65535 (lowest). When multiple rules match a packet, the highest-priority rule wins. If two rules have the same priority, the deny rule takes precedence. Best practice is to use priorities in the 1000-range for standard rules, reserving lower numbers for emergency overrides.

Service accounts can be used as targets and sources instead of network tags for stronger security. Unlike tags, which can be set by anyone with instance edit permission, service account-based targeting is controlled by IAM, preventing users from bypassing firewall rules by adding a tag to an unauthorized instance.

question.title: VPC Service Controls
question.scenario: Your organization needs to prevent data from Cloud Storage and BigQuery from being accessed or copied outside of your organization's network perimeter.
question.question-text: Which security feature should you implement?

choices.choice: VPC firewall rules with deny all egress
VPC Service Controls with a service perimeter

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: VPC Service Controls create a logical security perimeter around Google Cloud services that restricts data movement regardless of user permissions or network configuration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VPC Service Controls with a service perimeter (D) is the correct answer. A service perimeter defines a boundary around specified Google Cloud services (e.g., Cloud Storage, BigQuery) and projects, preventing data from being read, copied, or transferred outside the perimeter even by users with valid IAM permissions. Cloud Armor (A) protects against DDoS and application-layer attacks on load-balanced endpoints but does not control data movement between services. VPC firewall rules (B) control network traffic between VMs but cannot restrict access to Google-managed API endpoints. Private Google Access (C) enables VMs without external IPs to reach Google APIs but provides no data exfiltration controls.

ul.li: Service perimeters protect against data exfiltration by both external attackers and authorized insiders. Even a user with Storage Admin role cannot copy objects from a bucket inside the perimeter to a bucket outside it. This is a defense-in-depth layer that operates independently of and on top of IAM authorization.

Access levels define exceptions to the perimeter using context-aware conditions: allowed IP ranges (e.g., corporate egress IPs), device trust status (managed devices only), geographic origin, and identity attributes. Ingress and egress policies provide fine-grained rules for permitted cross-perimeter API calls.

Dry-run mode creates a perimeter that logs violations without blocking them, allowing you to analyze the impact before enforcement. Review dry-run audit logs to identify legitimate cross-perimeter traffic that needs access level or ingress/egress policy exceptions before switching to enforced mode.

VPC Service Controls support over 100 Google Cloud services including Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Pub/Sub, and AI Platform. When adding services to a perimeter, all projects containing those services must be inside the perimeter, or cross-project access will be blocked even within the same organization.

question.title: Organization Policies
question.scenario: Your security team wants to prevent anyone in the organization from creating Compute Engine instances with external IP addresses.
question.question-text: Which feature should you use to enforce this restriction?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Organization policies constrain how resources can be configured across the entire organization, independent of IAM permissions. They enforce guardrails that even administrators cannot bypass.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An organization policy constraint (A) is the correct tool. The compute.vmExternalIpAccess constraint prevents VMs from being assigned external IP addresses regardless of the user's IAM permissions. This is enforced at the resource creation level, meaning even an Owner cannot create a VM with an external IP when this constraint is active. IAM deny policies (B) block specific permissions but are harder to maintain for this use case. VPC firewall rules (C) control network traffic but do not prevent the assignment of external IPs. Custom IAM roles (D) could omit certain permissions but are easily bypassed by granting additional roles.

ul.li: Organization policies are fundamentally different from IAM. IAM controls who can perform actions (authentication and authorization), while organization policies control what resource configurations are allowed. Even a user with the Owner role is subject to organization policy constraints, making them a stronger enforcement mechanism for security guardrails.

The compute.vmExternalIpAccess constraint is a list constraint that specifies which VMs (by full resource name) are allowed to have external IPs. Setting the constraint to deny all at the organization level and then allowing specific exceptions at the project or folder level enables a default-deny posture with controlled exceptions.

Organization policies are inherited down the resource hierarchy (Organization > Folder > Project) and can be overridden at lower levels if the Organization Policy Administrator role is granted. Use hierarchical inheritance strategically: set restrictive defaults at the organization level and grant exceptions at lower levels only when justified.

Test organization policies before enforcement using the Policy Simulator or by applying them to a test folder first. Review the Organization Policy service logs in Cloud Audit Logs to identify which resource creation attempts would be denied, then create necessary exceptions before enforcing organization-wide.

question.title: Private Google Access
question.scenario: Your VM instances have no external IP addresses but need to access Google Cloud APIs and services like Cloud Storage.
question.question-text: Which feature enables these VMs to access Google APIs privately?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A subnet-level setting allows VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google Cloud API endpoints through Google's internal network without requiring external IPs or NAT.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private Google Access (C) enables VM instances with only internal IP addresses to communicate with Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, etc.) through Google's internal network. It is enabled per subnet and requires no additional infrastructure. Cloud NAT (B) provides outbound internet access for VMs without external IPs, which could technically reach Google APIs via the public internet, but it is not the intended or recommended solution for Google API access. VPC peering (A) connects two VPC networks privately but does not provide access to Google APIs. Cloud Interconnect (D) connects on-premises networks to Google Cloud, not internal VMs to Google APIs.

ul.li: Enable Private Google Access on a subnet with gcloud compute networks subnets update SUBNET --enable-private-ip-google-access --region=REGION. Traffic from VMs in that subnet to Google API endpoints (*.googleapis.com) is routed through Google's internal network without traversing the public internet, improving security and reducing egress costs.

Cloud NAT provides outbound internet connectivity for VMs without external IPs by performing network address translation at the VPC level. While VMs behind Cloud NAT can reach Google APIs through the public internet, this is less secure and less efficient than Private Google Access, which keeps traffic entirely within Google's network.

Private Service Connect extends the Private Google Access concept by creating private endpoints (internal IP addresses within your VPC) for specific Google APIs. This gives you DNS-level control, firewall rule targeting, and VPC Service Controls integration, providing more granular security than standard Private Google Access.

Combine Private Google Access with VPC Service Controls for maximum data security. Private Google Access ensures API traffic stays on Google's internal network, while VPC Service Controls prevent data exfiltration through those APIs. Together they create a strong security posture for sensitive workloads that must not expose data to the public internet.

question.title: Cloud Pub/Sub Integration
question.scenario: You need to build an event-driven architecture where multiple services consume the same messages independently at their own pace.
question.question-text: How should you configure Cloud Pub/Sub to support this pattern?

choices.choice: Create multiple topics, one per consuming service
Use pull delivery with a single subscription and distribute messages manually
Create one subscription shared across all services
Create one topic with multiple subscriptions, one per consuming service

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: In Pub/Sub's fan-out pattern, each subscription to a topic receives an independent copy of every published message, allowing multiple consumers to process the same events independently.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: One topic with multiple subscriptions (D) implements the fan-out messaging pattern. Each subscription receives a copy of every message published to the topic, and each consuming service processes messages from its own subscription at its own pace. A shared subscription (C) distributes messages among subscribers using load balancing, meaning each message goes to only one consumer, not all consumers. Multiple topics (A) would require the publisher to send to each topic, adding complexity and coupling. A single subscription with manual distribution (B) defeats the purpose of using Pub/Sub's built-in delivery mechanics and creates a single point of failure.

ul.li: The fan-out pattern (one topic, N subscriptions) ensures each consuming service sees every message independently. Messages remain in each subscription until acknowledged by that subscription's consumer, so a slow consumer does not block others. Pub/Sub retains unacknowledged messages for up to 7 days (configurable with message retention duration).

A shared subscription (multiple consumers pulling from one subscription) implements the competing consumers pattern, where Pub/Sub load-balances messages across the consumers. This is useful for scaling a single service horizontally but is the wrong pattern when multiple different services each need every message.

Dead-letter topics capture messages that fail processing after a configurable number of delivery attempts (max_delivery_attempts). Attach a dead-letter topic to each subscription to prevent poison messages from blocking the subscription. Monitor the dead-letter subscription for investigation and reprocessing of failed messages.

For ordering guarantees, use ordering keys when publishing. Messages with the same ordering key are delivered in order within a subscription. Without ordering keys, Pub/Sub may deliver messages out of order for higher throughput. If your consuming services require strict ordering, design your topic and ordering key strategy before implementation.

question.title: Workload Identity
question.scenario: Your GKE pods need to access Cloud Storage and BigQuery. You want to avoid using service account keys and follow security best practices.
question.question-text: Which feature allows GKE pods to authenticate to Google Cloud services without service account keys?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Workload Identity federates Kubernetes service account identity with Google Cloud IAM, allowing pods to authenticate to Google APIs using their Kubernetes identity without any key files.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Workload Identity (B) is the recommended way for GKE workloads to authenticate to Google Cloud services. It creates a trust relationship between a Kubernetes service account (KSA) and a Google Cloud service account (GSA), allowing pods running with that KSA to impersonate the GSA and obtain short-lived access tokens automatically. This eliminates the need to create, distribute, and rotate service account key files. Binary Authorization (A) verifies container image provenance before deployment but does not handle authentication. Pod Security Policies (C, deprecated in favor of Pod Security Standards) control pod-level security constraints. Network Policies (D) control pod-to-pod network traffic but do not address API authentication.

ul.li: Workload Identity setup requires three steps: enable Workload Identity on the cluster (--workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog), annotate the Kubernetes service account with the Google service account email (iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=GSA@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com), and grant the Workload Identity User role on the GSA to the KSA principal (serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA_NAME]).

Without Workload Identity, the common alternative is to mount a service account key file as a Kubernetes secret and set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable. This approach is insecure because key files are long-lived credentials that can be exfiltrated from the cluster and used externally. Workload Identity replaces this with short-lived, automatically rotated tokens.

Applications using Google Cloud client libraries with Application Default Credentials (ADC) work seamlessly with Workload Identity. The GKE metadata server intercepts metadata requests from the pod and returns access tokens for the mapped Google service account, requiring zero code changes in applications already using ADC.

Workload Identity provides pod-level identity isolation: different pods in the same namespace (or even on the same node) can have different Google Cloud service accounts based on their Kubernetes service account annotation. This is more granular than node-level service accounts, where all pods on a node share the same Google Cloud identity.

question.title: Cloud Monitoring Dashboards
question.scenario: Your team needs to visualize key performance metrics for your application including request latency, error rates, and resource utilization in a single view.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Monitoring feature should you use to create this visualization?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Custom dashboards in Cloud Monitoring allow you to arrange multiple metric visualizations (charts, gauges, scorecards) on a single page for comprehensive application observability.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A custom dashboard with multiple charts (C) is the correct feature for creating a unified view of multiple metrics. Dashboards support line charts, stacked area charts, bar charts, heatmaps, gauges, and scorecards, all on a single page with a synchronized time range selector. You can display request latency (p50, p95, p99), error rates (5xx count per minute), and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk) together. Logs Explorer (A) is for searching and browsing log entries, not metric visualization. Alerting policy summaries (B) show alert states but are not customizable metric dashboards. Service monitoring (D) provides SLO-focused views for individual services, not custom multi-metric layouts.

ul.li: Dashboards can be created in the Console UI or defined as JSON and managed as infrastructure-as-code using the Cloud Monitoring API or Terraform google_monitoring_dashboard resource. JSON-based dashboards can be version-controlled in Git, shared across projects via gcloud monitoring dashboards create --config-from-file, and deployed consistently across environments.

MQL (Monitoring Query Language) provides advanced metric querying capabilities within dashboard charts. MQL supports operations like fetch, filter, group_by, align, and outer_join, enabling complex derived metrics such as error rate percentages (errors divided by total requests) directly in the chart configuration without creating separate log-based metrics.

Dashboard widgets include log panels that display recent log entries alongside metric charts, enabling correlation between metric anomalies and log events on the same page. When a latency spike appears in a chart, the adjacent log panel can show corresponding error messages or warnings from the same time window.

Service monitoring provides SLO-based dashboards that track availability and latency against defined objectives (e.g., 99.9% of requests complete within 200ms). While powerful for SRE workflows, it is scoped to individual services with predefined SLI metrics, not the flexible multi-metric layout that custom dashboards provide for general operational visibility.
